prior_checkpoint.relationship: Adds saturation challenge batch 1: five new qualifying whole-text papers and fifteen normalized atomic observations.

mission_boundary.core: Data-center buildout, project states, campus scale, siting, construction and commissioning, disclosed versus energized capacity, geographic concentration, facility resource use, and project-pipeline interpretation.
permanent_boundaries: A project registry is a coverage-limited sample, not a national fleet census.
Published, design, contracted, connected, energized, IT, and average-load megawatts are distinct states.
Current status of named projects remains deterministic runtime evidence.
An academic corpus teaches calibrated reasoning and language; it does not replace live project data.

completion_contract.saturation_rule: After adequate foundation coverage, two consecutive five-paper batches must each add no more than two genuinely new generalizable observations and reopen no material gap.
completion_contract.long_form_requirement: Approximately 10 to 15 substantial passage analyses from one or two qualifying academic texts.
completion_contract.admission_gate: Direct fit, JIF at least 2.0, verified whole text, normalized extraction, durable provenance.

journal_gate_verification.verification_note: Current 2025 JIF independently visible in journal metrics; publisher page is durable target.

journal_gate_verification.journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research

journal_gate_verification.verification_note: Current JIF corroborated; publisher page is durable target.

official_admissions.title: Recalibrating global data center energy-use estimates
official_admissions.study_type: bottom-up global energy-accounting synthesis and policy forum

sections_reviewed: 2010 to 2018 service, equipment and energy trends

rhetoric.claim_path: The paper rejects traffic- or workload-only extrapolation, integrates equipment, virtualization, storage, network, PUE and market-structure data, and presents a conditional near-term efficiency scenario.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Energy is decomposed across servers, storage, network equipment, and infrastructure; compute instances, IP traffic, storage capacity and electricity are separate quantities.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: From 2010 to 2018, estimated compute instances rose 550% while global data-center electricity rose about 6%, from roughly 194 to 205 TWh; energy per compute instance fell about 20% annually.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: The result depends on shifts from traditional facilities toward cloud and hyperscale sites, virtualization, device efficiency, storage density, and PUE; practical PUE improvement approaches a floor near highly optimized hyperscale operation.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is a bottom-up accounting synthesis and conditional near-term scenario, not proof that future AI load growth will remain energy-flat.
limitations: Public bottom-up data on facility types, locations, equipment and efficiency remain incomplete.
Long-run technical limits and disruptive technologies are uncertain.
The scenario requires continued efficiency progress and policy effort.
anti_patterns: Do not scale electricity directly from IP traffic, workload, storage or compute-instance growth.
Do not turn a conditional near-term plateau scenario into a permanent forecast.
Do not use PUE alone as a measure of useful computing service.

official_admissions.title: Data centre water consumption
official_admissions.study_type: critical review and measurement-framework analysis

rhetoric.claim_path: The article expands data-center environmental accounting beyond energy, separates direct cooling water from electricity-generation water, evaluates measurement metrics and disclosure gaps, and links water impact to local scarcity and siting.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Withdrawal differs from consumption; site WUE differs from source-inclusive WUE; both divide water by IT-equipment energy and therefore depend on consistent site, time and grid boundaries.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The article reports that a traditional 1 MW facility can consume around 25.5 million litres annually and that higher chilled-water temperatures can materially reduce cooling cost, but both figures are technology- and climate-conditioned.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Cooling demand and feasible technology vary with ambient climate, season, water source, electricity generation mix, facility design and equipment tolerance.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: The paper synthesizes published and corporate data; it does not estimate a universal causal effect of siting or cooling changes.
limitations: Operator water disclosure is sparse and often not attributed specifically to data centers.
Source-water intensity factors vary by technology and geography and become stale as grids change.
Customer migration to cloud can reduce visibility into the resources behind purchased services.
anti_patterns: Do not equate withdrawal with consumption.
Do not call site WUE a complete water footprint.
Do not compare vendor water totals without organizational and methodological boundaries.

official_admissions.title: Using life cycle assessment to drive innovation for sustainable cool clouds
official_admissions.study_type: provider-authored cradle-to-grave comparative life-cycle assessment

rhetoric.claim_path: The study defines a cradle-to-grave functional unit, compares three advanced cooling designs against air cooling, decomposes use-phase and embodied impacts, and uses the tradeoffs to inform early design choices.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Impacts are annualized and normalized per virtual core; the boundary includes building shell, workload, servers, racks or tanks, support equipment, grid electricity, water, fluids and end-of-life treatment.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The modeled advanced-cooling designs reduce GHG emissions by roughly 15–21%, primary energy by 15–20%, and blue-water consumption by 31–52% per virtual core-year against the modeled air-cooled reference.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Results shift with grid mix, server lifetime, density, cooling fluid, maintenance model, regulatory treatment, and whether use-phase or embodied impacts dominate.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This comparative LCA estimates impacts under a specified provider design model; it is not measured fleet-wide realized savings or a market-adoption result.
limitations: Specific cooling-fluid, data-center-equipment and semiconductor inventories were missing or outdated and required proxies.
The paper uses a pedigree matrix rather than a complete quantitative uncertainty distribution.
Provider design assumptions and functional-unit choices condition transferability.
anti_patterns: Do not compare cooling systems without the same functional unit and life-cycle boundary.
Do not describe modeled per-core reductions as measured total-fleet reductions.
Do not ignore embodied burdens that become more prominent as operational electricity decarbonizes.

official_admissions.title: Decarbonising digital infrastructure and urban sustainability in the case of data centres
official_admissions.study_type: mixed-method urban infrastructure and sustainability case study

whole_text.provenance: Whole-text audit completed during Compute recovery and reclassified here for direct Data Centers use.
sections_reviewed: technology, regulation, finance, infrastructure and workforce findings

rhetoric.claim_path: The study challenges digital dematerialization, maps data-center growth into a land-, water- and carbon-constrained urban system, and identifies implementation gaps across technology, policy, finance, infrastructure and people.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: The evidence is a non-exhaustive asset landscape, policy and corporate documents, 59 semi-structured interviews, and two validation workshops totaling 150 participants.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Counts describe the qualitative evidence base, not a representative estimate of all operators or projects.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Tropical climate, grid carbon, land and water scarcity, connectivity, sovereignty, financing, brownfield status and operator risk tolerance change feasible transitions.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is a mixed-method Singapore case, not a causal technology evaluation. Corporate claims and project projections remain stakeholder evidence.
limitations: The asset landscape is non-exhaustive.
The institutional and physical regime is Singapore-specific.
Cross-border relocation can shift rather than remove environmental burdens.
anti_patterns: Do not treat PUE, renewable certificates or a green-building label as complete sustainability.
Do not treat announced green finance as realized low-carbon infrastructure.
Do not infer regional burden reduction when restrictions displace capacity across a border.

official_admissions.title: Maximizing waste heat recovery from a building-integrated edge data center
official_admissions.study_type: physical pilot parameterization plus validated thermal simulation and workload-placement optimization

whole_text.provenance: Whole-text audit completed during Compute recovery and reclassified here for direct Data Centers use.

rhetoric.claim_path: The paper measures a pilot rack, validates a thermal model, searches workload placements with a fast evaluator, and reports modeled heat-recovery gains before delimiting operational deployment.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: A 32-server single-rack pilot supports up to 12 kW; optimization compares modeled placements against random placement under specified flow and load conditions.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The fast evaluator reports R-squared 0.93 and RMSE 1.44 degrees C; the validated model estimates up to 17.1% more recovered heat and up to 53.2% lower transferred cooling load under selected conditions.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Benefits decline as IT load rises and placement flexibility disappears; geometry, hardware homogeneity, cooling configuration, workload colocation and thermal limits condition results.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: Physical measurements parameterize the model, but optimization gains are simulated rather than measured production-fleet energy savings.
limitations: Single-rack scale and homogeneous hardware.
No production scheduler deployment.
No measured net building or grid energy outcome.
anti_patterns: Do not collapse experimental parameterization, model validation, simulated policy gain and production deployment.
Do not call recovered heat net electricity savings.
Do not transfer low-load placement gains into saturation conditions.

official_admissions.title: Data center growth in the United States: Decoupling the demand for services from electricity use
official_admissions.study_type: twenty-year bottom-up United States stock-and-flow electricity model with scenarios

sections_reviewed: server, storage and network stock model

rhetoric.claim_path: The paper reconstructs equipment stocks and operational characteristics by space type, derives useful workload with full-power equivalents, and contrasts frozen-efficiency, current-trend and best-practice scenarios.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Installed servers, full-power-equivalent workload, floor-space type, PUE, utilization and annual electricity are modeled separately; neither installed base nor electricity alone measures service demand.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Recent United States data-center electricity demand was nearly steady around 70 billion kWh, while the same projected 2020 workload spans roughly 135 billion kWh between frozen-efficiency and best-practice scenarios and nearly a factor of four across the full scenario range.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Efficiency, virtualization and consolidation opportunities differ across server closets, rooms, localized facilities, mid-tier sites and hyperscale facilities.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is calibrated bottom-up accounting plus conditional scenarios, not a forecast that fixes post-2020 electricity demand.
limitations: Input data are uneven across space and equipment types.
Scenario outcomes depend on adoption rates for efficiency and consolidation.
The analysis does not establish post-2020 AI-specific demand.
anti_patterns: Do not equate installed servers with delivered workload.
Do not treat a scenario envelope as a point forecast.
Do not apply hyperscale efficiency to the whole heterogeneous stock.

official_admissions.title: Assessing the environmental impact of data centres part 1: Background, energy use and metrics
official_admissions.study_type: critical literature review of data-center energy, environmental impact and metrics

rhetoric.claim_path: The review traces why operational energy and PUE became dominant, evaluates later carbon, water and compute metrics, and shows why no single operational metric represents whole-system sustainability.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: PUE is total facility energy divided by IT-equipment energy; other metrics use different numerators, boundaries and service denominators and therefore are not interchangeable.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Reported sector totals and facility ratios vary with inventory scope, time, site type and measurement practice; the review treats them as boundary-conditioned rather than universal constants.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Facilities range from single racks and server rooms to warehouse-scale sites, with different cooling, redundancy, occupancy and measurement feasibility.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is a critical review of metrics and evidence, not a measured intervention study.
limitations: The literature and disclosure base was incomplete and rapidly changing.
Single-issue metrics omit cross-impact and life-cycle effects.
Metric definitions and measurement points are not always harmonized.
anti_patterns: Do not call PUE a sustainability score.
Do not compare ratios without aligned boundaries and time periods.
Do not infer lower total impact from improvement in one operational metric.

official_admissions.title: Data Center Energy Evaluation Tool Development and Analysis of Power Usage Effectiveness with Different Economizer Types in Various Climate Zones
official_admissions.study_type: engineering-tool development and comparative climate/economizer simulation

rhetoric.claim_path: The study develops a reduced-input energy tool, verifies it against established simulation software, and uses it to compare PUE under cooling and economizer choices across climates.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: PUE is calculated from modeled IT and support energy under aligned weather, setpoint, load and cooling-system assumptions.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Predicted PUE and cooling savings change materially with outdoor temperature and humidity, economizer type and control limits rather than inhering in the equipment label alone.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Air-side and water-side economizers have different feasible hours and performance across climate zones and setpoints.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: Software agreement verifies implementation consistency; it is not field validation of realized annual operating cost or environmental impact.
limitations: Capital cost and maintenance are excluded.
Water use and heat-reuse value are excluded.
The modeled system does not cover all liquid-cooling or rear-door configurations.
anti_patterns: Do not generalize an economizer result across climates.
Do not treat software-to-software agreement as production validation.
Do not infer whole-system sustainability from modeled PUE.

official_admissions.title: Thermal Performance Evaluation of a Data Center Cooling System under Fault Conditions
official_admissions.study_type: project-specific transient thermal analysis and commissioning-oriented fault evaluation

rhetoric.claim_path: The study models loss-of-cooling faults in an actual 20 MW project configuration and translates transient temperature behavior into backup activation and commissioning requirements.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: The key outcome is time until server-inlet temperature exceeds the specified allowable envelope under defined chilled-water and supply-air starting conditions.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: At chilled-water/supply-air conditions no higher than about 17/24 degrees C, allowable time was about 320 seconds; warmer initial conditions caused faster temperature rise, supporting backup activation within 300 seconds.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Thermal ride-through depends on starting temperature, air volume, thermal mass, fault type, redundancy and whether cooling components share UPS protection.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: The project geometry is real, but fault outcomes are transient simulations used for design and commissioning rather than measured fleet outage statistics.
limitations: Results depend on the studied 20 MW configuration.
Model assumptions govern thermal mass and airflow response.
The study evaluates a bounded fault interval, not long-duration resilience.
anti_patterns: Do not call installed redundancy verified resilience before integrated fault testing.
Do not transfer a ride-through time across thermal starting states.
Do not assume IT UPS protection also protects cooling.

official_admissions.title: The Energy-Saving Potential of Air-Side Economisers in Modular Data Centres: Analysis of Opportunities and Risks in Different Climates
official_admissions.study_type: dynamic simulation of a modular data center across four climate regimes

sections_reviewed: Stockholm, Dubai, San Francisco and Singapore cases

rhetoric.claim_path: The paper models an air-side economizer for a 90 kW modular facility and tests its opportunity and risk under four distinct climates.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Energy savings and PUE are annual modeled outcomes relative to the same mechanical-cooling base case and specified control envelope.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The model estimates savings as high as about 86% in a favorable moderate climate, while hot-dry and hot-humid climates provide much smaller opportunities.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Temperature, humidity, enthalpy, particulate risk, control strategy and climate determine free-cooling hours and suitability.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: The base model is checked against published PUE data, but climate comparisons remain simulations rather than multi-site billing measurements.
limitations: Validation lacks detailed facility billing and infiltration measurements.
Contaminant and reliability risks are not fully quantified.
The 90 kW modular geometry is not a hyperscale campus.
anti_patterns: Do not apply the maximum modeled saving to all climates.
Do not equate a modular prototype with fleet-average performance.
Do not omit air-quality and humidity constraints from free-cooling claims.

official_admissions.title: Flexibility-Based Energy and Demand Management in Data Centers: A Case Study for Cloud Computing
official_admissions.study_type: flexibility review, management-framework design and lab-grade cloud testbed experiment

sections_reviewed: IT, cooling and storage flexibility mechanisms

rhetoric.claim_path: The paper separates kWh minimization from kW peak reduction, maps technical flexibility to contracts, implements management systems, and evaluates them on a lab-grade cloud testbed.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Overall energy and interval peak power are different objectives; flexibility is the feasible, time-bounded change subject to workload, hardware and SLA constraints.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The reported case results include roughly 33% overall energy saving and 50% demand-response peak reduction under the tested federation and workload conditions.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Deferrability, migration, consolidation, thermal headroom, storage state, workload shape and contract terms determine deliverable flexibility.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: The control mechanisms are experimentally evaluated at lab-grade scale; federation-wide savings are not evidence of unrestricted production-fleet response.
limitations: Lab-grade scale limits external validity.
Savings depend on workload and baseline construction.
QoS and contractual acceptability constrain response.
anti_patterns: Do not equate nameplate load with dispatchable flexibility.
Do not conflate kW peak reduction with kWh energy savings.
Do not ignore SLA and workload consequences.

official_admissions.title: Data Centers Optimized Integration with Multi-Energy Grids: Test Cases and Results in Operational Environment
official_admissions.study_type: multi-site operational pilots and test cases for electrical, thermal and IT flexibility

rhetoric.claim_path: The study implements a flexibility-management architecture and demonstrates separate electrical, thermal and workload scenarios in operational pilots and test cases.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Electrical load, recoverable heat and movable IT work are separate profiles; reported flexibility is scenario- and interval-specific.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The test cases show that renewable availability can be coupled to storage and load migration, but the achievable level changes with QoS and production conditions.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: On-site generation, battery state, workload mobility, network delay, heat demand and site topology change the feasible response.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: Operational pilots establish technical feasibility at their tested scale, not a universal market-wide flexibility quantity.
limitations: Pilot and micro-data-center scales are not full campus deployments.
Economic and regulatory participation conditions vary by market.
Heat-reuse results require a coincident local sink.
anti_patterns: Do not add electrical, thermal and IT flexibility as if they were identical units.
Do not call available waste heat useful heat without a matched sink.
Do not extrapolate pilot response to nameplate campus load.

official_admissions.title: How Data Centers Have Come to Matter: Governing the Spatial and Environmental Footprint of the 'Digital Gateway to Europe'
official_admissions.journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
official_admissions.study_type: qualitative urban-infrastructure and policy-history case study

rhetoric.claim_path: The paper traces how a spatially concentrated data-center sector moved from politically obscured enabling infrastructure to contested land, power and heat infrastructure, followed by moratoria and policy reform.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: The unit of analysis is a metropolitan governance regime and its clustered campuses, institutions and policy fields, not a national facility census.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Facility counts, campus maps and policy events support the historical case; they do not estimate a general causal effect of data-center entry.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Local grid scarcity, land constraints, municipal competition, national policy, connectivity and heat-network institutions determine the governance response.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: Process tracing supports a contextual account of politicization and regulation, not a transportable numerical treatment effect.
limitations: Amsterdam is an unusually mature and concentrated gateway market.
Policy documents and interviews reflect institutional perspectives.
The case cannot serve as a global fleet inventory.
anti_patterns: Do not describe cloud infrastructure as placeless.
Do not infer national capacity from one metropolitan cluster.
Do not count planned heat reuse as delivered heat without network and demand realization.

official_admissions.title: The environmental footprint of data centers in the United States
official_admissions.study_type: bottom-up geospatial operational water and carbon footprint model

rhetoric.claim_path: The study links facilities to grids, power plants, water utilities, wastewater treatment and watersheds to estimate location-specific operational water and carbon footprints and siting tradeoffs.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Direct cooling water, indirect power-generation water, water-treatment energy and GHG emissions are attributed through explicit operational boundaries; a hypothetical 1 MW site is used for comparable siting intensities.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: About one-fifth of servers direct water footprint is in moderately to highly water-stressed watersheds, nearly half are at least partly powered by plants in water-stressed regions, and modeled 2018 operations account for about 31.5 million tons CO2-equivalent, around 0.5% of United States emissions.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Grid mix, watershed stress, cooling practice, utility territory and facility location produce large geographic variation and tradeoffs among water, scarcity-weighted water and carbon.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is spatial attribution and counterfactual siting analysis, not observation of identical facilities randomly relocated.
limitations: Facility locations and server counts are coverage-limited inputs.
Grid and utility attribution uses modeled connections and averages.
Operational scope excludes full embodied and construction impacts.
anti_patterns: Do not treat a mapped facility list as a complete fleet census.
Do not report national averages as local burden.
Do not equate ordinary water volume with scarcity-weighted impact.

official_admissions.title: A Circular Economy for the Data Centre Industry: Using Design Methods to Address the Challenge of Whole System Sustainability in a Unique Industrial Sector
official_admissions.study_type: project case study using sector survey, nine expert interviews and design-process evaluation

sections_reviewed: Design Thinking and Double Diamond methods

rhetoric.claim_path: The paper frames the data-center equipment chain as ten siloed subsectors, applies whole-system design methods in CEDaCI, and evaluates early project engagement and perceived impact through a 44-person survey and nine senior-expert interviews.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Evidence measures participant engagement, perceptions and project-process outputs; it does not measure sector-wide recovered material or avoided lifecycle impact.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The empirical evaluation includes 44 survey participants and nine senior experts, with 17 interview themes; authors explicitly state that creating a sectoral circular economy in three and a half years is unrealistic.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Designers, manufacturers, operators, users, refurbishers, asset-disposition firms and recyclers have different information, incentives and technical constraints.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: The evidence supports early awareness, engagement and design-process learning, not proof of completed industry transformation.
limitations: Small, project-engaged samples risk positive-selection bias.
Outcomes are early-stage and largely process or perception measures.
Material-flow and avoided-impact outcomes were not yet observed sector-wide.
anti_patterns: Do not call project participation completed circularity.
Do not infer recovered material from design-tool availability.
Do not optimize one lifecycle stage without tracing effects on the other subsectors.

official_admissions.title: Environmental footprints of the data center service sector in Sweden
official_admissions.study_type: national footprint model plus GIS multi-criteria site-suitability analysis

sections_reviewed: renewable, free-cooling, heat-sink and water-risk criteria

rhetoric.claim_path: The study constructs a Swedish data-center inventory from heterogeneous public and survey sources, estimates sector energy, water and GHG footprints, then scores existing and prospective locations with a multi-criteria GIS tool.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Facility environmental estimates and the site-suitability index are separate outputs; the latter combines renewable access, free cooling, excess-heat receivers and resilience to water shortage.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The model estimates roughly 5.4% of Swedish electricity, 42 million cubic metres of annual water and 0.3% of national GHG emissions for the sector; 68 facilities score at or below 45% on the authors site-suitability index.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Northern and southern locations differ in climate, geology, grid, heat sinks and water risk, while missing facility data require proxies.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is inventory estimation and suitability scoring, not causal evidence that relocating a facility produces the modeled benefit.
limitations: The facility inventory is assembled from questionnaires, permits, corporate sites and open repositories rather than mandatory standardized reporting.
Missing facility parameters require assumptions and imputation.
A composite suitability score inherits selected criteria and weights.
anti_patterns: Do not treat the assembled list as a certified fleet census.
Do not read a suitability score as actual operating performance.
Do not compare composite scores without preserving criteria and weights.

official_admissions.title: Planning data center locations in Swedish municipalities: A comparative case study of Luleå and Stockholm
official_admissions.study_type: comparative urban-planning case study

sections_reviewed: municipal spatial and energy planning evidence

rhetoric.claim_path: The paper compares how two municipalities integrate data centers into spatial and energy planning and identifies determinants of municipal adaptive capacity.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: The unit of analysis is the municipal energy-spatial system; determinants include electricity and water infrastructure, heat-producer and user diversity, land-use diversity and property fragmentation.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The result is a structured comparative judgment that Stockholm exhibits higher adaptive capacity than Luleå, not a causal effect size or universal location ranking.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Climate, energy availability, ownership fragmentation, district-heating institutions and municipal authority change feasible integration.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: Comparative case evidence supports planning mechanisms and contrasts, not a general causal ranking of all municipalities.
limitations: Two Swedish municipalities limit transferability.
Planning evidence does not itself establish completed infrastructure or realized heat exchange.
Adaptive-capacity assessment depends on the selected framework and evidence.
anti_patterns: Do not equate municipal plan adoption with energized capacity.
Do not call waste heat beneficial without an integrated user and network.
Do not rank sites on climate alone while ignoring governance and infrastructure.

official_admissions.title: The relationship between data centers and the climate is a systems challenge: a spatial analysis of United States data centers
official_admissions.study_type: national geospatial operational-risk analysis

rhetoric.claim_path: The paper combines a coverage-limited site inventory with heat, water-stress and grid-emissions layers to evaluate environment-to-facility operational risks and facility-to-environment burdens.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: The analysis locates more than 2,400 facilities and attaches regional environmental-risk indicators; site presence does not encode MW, operating state or utilization.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Spatial clusters and risk categories reveal that many facilities face heat or water stress and materially different grid emissions, but the paper does not convert site counts into fleet load.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Local climate, watershed conditions, grid mix and regional clustering jointly determine risk; those variables can be correlated rather than independent.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is cross-sectional spatial association and risk screening, not causal impact evaluation.
limitations: Commercial and public facility inventories may omit, duplicate or misclassify sites.
Location-only records lack standardized capacity and operating state.
Regional indicators do not substitute for facility operating measurements.
anti_patterns: Do not multiply site counts by a generic MW value.
Do not call proximity to risk realized outage or damage.
Do not infer causation from spatial clustering.

official_admissions.title: Data centres as a source of flexibility for power systems
official_admissions.study_type: critical review and case-based flexibility synthesis

rhetoric.claim_path: The review maps data-center assets and workload controls to power-system services and tests their plausibility against case examples and market requirements.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Flexibility must specify direction, response time, duration, recovery, energy capacity, availability window and service baseline; asset capacity is not automatically deliverable response.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Case values vary by asset and market and are presented as examples rather than a fleet aggregate; the authors report no new dataset for the review itself.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: UPS topology, battery sizing, generator rules, workload type, QoS/SLA, electricity-market design and regulation change availability.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: The review supports technical potential and bounded case feasibility, not a measured national dispatchable total.
limitations: No new data were used.
Case studies are heterogeneous and may be selectively reported.
Regulatory and market transferability is limited.
anti_patterns: Do not sum all asset ratings as simultaneous flexibility.
Do not omit response duration and recovery.
Do not treat technical potential as market-qualified availability.

official_admissions.title: A Review of Data Centers Energy Consumption and Reliability Modeling
official_admissions.study_type: systematic technical review of component energy and reliability models

rhetoric.claim_path: The review classifies component energy models and analytical or simulation reliability methods across 193 papers, then identifies missing power-conditioning, cooling-reliability and failure-data evidence.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Component power consumption, component reliability, degraded operation, service availability and tier classification are different model layers.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Internal power-conditioning losses can approach 10% in cited configurations, but the review emphasizes that parameter availability can matter more than nominal model accuracy for usable assessment.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Topology, redundancy, component dependence, repair assumptions, cooling architecture and failure data determine modeled reliability.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is a model-taxonomy and research-gap review, not measured failure-rate estimation for the data-center fleet.
limitations: Failure data are scarce, particularly for cooling and component dependencies.
Reviewed models use inconsistent assumptions and validation.
Tier labels do not fully specify operating or degraded-state behavior.
anti_patterns: Do not equate tier classification with measured availability.
Do not assume independent component failures where systems are coupled.
Do not optimize energy without testing reliability consequences.

official_admissions.title: Sources of data center energy estimates: A comprehensive review
official_admissions.study_type: systematic provenance and methodology review of energy estimates

rhetoric.claim_path: The review traces original energy estimates rather than repeated citations, classifies their methods and boundaries, and evaluates how methodological opacity propagates divergent public claims.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Energy estimates differ by included facility types, equipment, geography, year, electricity boundary, workload proxy and whether the value is observed, modeled or forecast.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Only 31% of reviewed sources were peer-reviewed publications and 38% were non-peer-reviewed reports; many sources did not disclose enough method to reproduce or compare estimates.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Global and national estimates rely on different mixtures of direct measurement, installed-stock models, traffic proxies and scenario assumptions.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is evidence-provenance analysis; it does not select a timeless correct energy total.
limitations: The review is bounded to original estimates located for 2007–2021.
Commercial and confidential sources limit validation.
Published methods and classifications can become stale as facility mix changes.
anti_patterns: Do not cite a secondary repetition as independent evidence.
Do not compare totals without reconstructing their scope and year.
Do not average incompatible estimates to manufacture precision.

official_admissions.title: Building Accurate Energy-Use Statistics for Data Centers
official_admissions.study_type: measurement-framework and policy analysis

rhetoric.claim_path: The paper diagnoses structural gaps in data-center energy statistics and proposes treating data centers as a distinct end-use sector with standardized, coordinated reporting.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Reported 2020 global consumption ranges from 196 to 1,200 TWh because indirect proxies, sector definitions, aggregation and reporting boundaries differ.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The more-than-sixfold estimate range is evidence of statistical architecture failure, not physical volatility within the same defined population.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: National statistical systems, operator disclosure, facility definitions, grid boundaries and temporal granularity differ.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is a diagnostic and policy-framework paper, not a new meter-level global census.
limitations: The proposed reporting regime is normative and not yet universally implemented.
Operator confidentiality and classification differences remain barriers.
Harmonized reporting would still require capacity and operating-state fields.
anti_patterns: Do not collapse divergent definitions into a midpoint.
Do not use traffic or revenue as unqualified electricity proxies.
Do not call modeled demand metered consumption.

official_admissions.title: Environmental impact and net-zero pathways for sustainable artificial intelligence servers in the USA
official_admissions.study_type: open-source bottleneck-based projection with spatial energy-water-carbon scenarios

rhetoric.claim_path: The study projects AI-server shipments from a supply-chain bottleneck, translates them into operational power with utilization assumptions, allocates them geographically using current and in-construction large-site records, and tests efficiency, siting and grid scenarios.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Rated AI-server capacity, shipments, active-server ratio, processor utilization, facility PUE/WUE, grid factors and annual footprints are separate layers.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Modeled indirect water is 71% of total; best modeled industry practices reduce energy, water and carbon about 12%, 32% and 11%, while spatial scenarios produce much larger positive or adverse changes.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Manufacturing capacity, chip design, adoption, training/inference mix, site distribution, cooling and grid development all drive the scenario range.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: These are transparent scenario projections, not observed 2024–2030 fleet outcomes.
limitations: Spatial allocation uses major purchasers current and in-construction large facilities and building area as a proxy.
The distribution is held constant after considering construction uncertainty.
Market, geopolitical, algorithmic and full embodied impacts are outside scope.
anti_patterns: Do not call in-construction building area energized AI load.
Do not treat supply-chain capacity as deployed servers.
Do not present a scenario pathway as a realized net-zero trajectory.

official_admissions.title: A review of data center cooling technology, operating conditions and the corresponding low-grade waste heat recovery opportunities
official_admissions.study_type: thermodynamic review of cooling architectures and heat-recovery pathways

rhetoric.claim_path: The review matches data-center heat-stream temperature and form to the operating requirements of recovery technologies and distinguishes retrofit from co-designed siting opportunities.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Waste-heat quantity, temperature quality, recoverable fraction, usable delivered heat and displaced primary energy are distinct quantities.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Many useful processes require roughly 45–60 degrees C or higher and heat degrades with distance; liquid and two-phase cooling expose more recovery options than low-temperature air cooling.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Cooling architecture, outlet temperature, distance, sink demand, retrofit status and working fluid govern feasibility.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: The review identifies thermodynamic and engineering suitability, not measured adoption or net savings across operating fleets.
limitations: Several technologies were developmental at publication.
Economic and regulatory conditions are site-specific.
A technically recoverable stream may lack a coincident buyer.
anti_patterns: Do not equate rejected heat with useful delivered heat.
Do not ignore temperature grade and distance.
Do not transfer new-build co-location options to legacy retrofits.

official_admissions.title: Global data center expansion and human health: A call for empirical research
official_admissions.study_type: peer-reviewed perspective and research-agenda synthesis

rhetoric.claim_path: The perspective maps plausible health pathways from noise, backup generation, grid emissions, heat and water burdens and explicitly calls for exposure and epidemiological research.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Internal equipment noise, property-line exposure, intermittent generator testing, chronic grid emissions and modeled population health burdens are different evidence levels.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The paper cites internal noise values up to 96 dBA and model-based future health burdens, but presents them as motivating evidence rather than direct community epidemiology.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Facility design, generator fuel and testing, grid mix, distance, land use, workforce exposure and baseline community vulnerability change risk.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is an agenda-setting perspective; most community health pathways remain hypotheses or modeled risks rather than established facility-specific causal effects.
limitations: Direct epidemiological evidence near data centers is sparse.
Many cited figures come from models or non-data-center analogues.
Exposure boundaries and affected populations require measurement.
anti_patterns: Do not convert internal dBA into neighborhood exposure.
Do not report modeled future deaths as observed cases.
Do not omit baseline vulnerability and cumulative exposure.

official_admissions.title: The Water Footprint of Data Centers
official_admissions.study_type: preliminary system water-footprint accounting and uncertainty synthesis

rhetoric.claim_path: The paper expands data-center water accounting beyond on-site cooling to include the water embodied in electricity generation and demonstrates a very wide result range.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Facility water per unit of energy and outbound-traffic water per gigabyte are distinct functional units built from direct and indirect components.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Reported estimates span 1,047–151,061 cubic metres per terajoule and 1–205 litres per gigabyte, with electricity-related water often dominating.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Electricity portfolio, generation technology, cooling architecture, climate and traffic assumptions control the result.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is preliminary accounting built from heterogeneous secondary factors, not metered fleet evidence.
limitations: Input uncertainty is large.
Traffic-normalized results depend on an unstable service denominator.
Local water stress is not represented by volume alone.
anti_patterns: Do not equate on-site water with total water footprint.
Do not transfer a global-average intensity to a specific grid.
Do not present the range midpoint as a measured typical site.

official_admissions.title: Data center design and location: Consequences for electricity use and greenhouse-gas emissions
official_admissions.study_type: prototype-building energy simulation across climate, mechanical design and grid-emissions conditions

rhetoric.claim_path: Climate-conditioned building simulations compare mechanical designs and then combine electricity results with regional emissions factors.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: IT energy, HVAC energy, total facility energy, PUE and grid-attributed GHG emissions are separate outputs.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Effective widespread economizer use is modeled to reduce sector electricity demand by about 20–25%, equivalent to roughly 13–17 TWh per year in the modeled national technical-potential calculation.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Climate, humidity controls, data-center space type, cooling design and electricity mix change savings and emissions.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: The national figure is modeled technical potential under adoption assumptions, not observed realized savings.
limitations: Prototype operation cannot represent every facility.
Grid emissions vary by location and time.
Adoption, commissioning and maintenance affect realization.
anti_patterns: Do not treat economizer potential as automatic operating savings.
Do not infer emissions from PUE without grid context.
Do not transfer a climate result without the mechanical-design regime.

official_admissions.title: Data centers as a source of dynamic flexibility in smart grids
official_admissions.study_type: technical-economic feasibility analysis and simulation of dual-purpose UPS battery response

rhetoric.claim_path: The authors test whether bidirectional UPS systems can supply primary-frequency response while preserving their protection role.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Stored energy, power-electronics rating, response time, state of charge, reserve requirement and market revenue are distinct constraints.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Because primary regulation is relatively energy-light and UPS batteries are sized for redundancy, the modeled system has ample energy under bounded participation and meets reaction-speed requirements.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: UPS topology, battery chemistry and age, reserved state of charge, activation history, market rules and reliability policy govern feasibility.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: The paper demonstrates modeled technical-economic feasibility, not fleet-wide dispatch participation or realized revenue.
limitations: Battery aging depends on the activation profile.
Market economics are jurisdiction-specific.
Protection obligations remain lexically prior to grid service.
anti_patterns: Do not equate installed battery energy with dispatchable flexibility.
Do not ignore the reliability reserve.
Do not transfer market revenue without product rules and prices.

official_admissions.title: Optimized data center site selection—mesoclimatic effects on data center energy consumption and costs
official_admissions.study_type: one-kilometre-resolution mesoclimate and reference-facility cooling simulation

rhetoric.claim_path: The study asks whether small within-country location changes create material cooling-energy differences and models a reference facility across Baden-Württemberg.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: The reported percentage savings refer to the recirculating chiller component relative to a baseline site, not automatically to total facility electricity.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Within a 10 km location radius, modeled annual chiller savings average 9.12% and reach 56.58%; wider location freedom produces larger modeled savings.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Topography, one-kilometre temperature data, chiller behavior, selected baseline and permitted relocation radius govern results.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: This is modeled site-selection potential for a reference design, not an observed operating-fleet effect.
limitations: The reference design fixes many operational variables.
Land, grid, fiber and permitting constraints are outside the cooling optimization.
Component savings should not be silently recast as PUE or total-site savings.
anti_patterns: Do not ignore mesoclimate within a nominal market.
Do not turn component savings into facility savings.
Do not optimize climate while omitting other siting constraints.

official_admissions.title: Toward climate neutral data centers: Greenhouse gas inventory, scenarios, and strategies
official_admissions.study_type: GHG Protocol-aligned generic inventory and 2030 scenario/sensitivity model

rhetoric.claim_path: A generic Germany-based facility inventory traces operational and value-chain emissions, then tests efficiency, utilization and electricity scenarios through 2030.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: Location-based Scope 2, market-based procurement, Scope 3 embodied emissions and net-zero claims require distinct accounting fields.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: The illustrative baseline projects energy use up 20% and total GHG up 13%; combined operational measures and renewable electricity can cut emissions materially but do not eliminate all value-chain emissions.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Equipment stock, utilization, PUE, electricity factors, component lifetimes and scope boundary drive the model.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: The scenario is explanatory and sensitivity-based; it is not a forecast for the German or global fleet.
limitations: The model is deliberately simplified.
Facility categories and applications are not fully differentiated.
Many inputs remain uncertain or nontransparent.
anti_patterns: Do not define neutrality with an undisclosed scope boundary.
Do not treat renewable procurement as elimination of Scope 3.
Do not generalize an illustrative facility to a fleet forecast.

atomic_observations.observation: Service demand, compute instances, storage capacity, network traffic, installed equipment and facility electricity are separate stocks or flows and cannot be extrapolated one-for-one.
PUE describes facility overhead relative to IT energy; it does not measure useful computation, service quality, utilization or total environmental burden.
An efficiency trajectory supports a conditional scenario only while its technological, structural and policy drivers continue; it is not a permanent law.
Do not forecast data-center electricity by multiplying a historical energy estimate by traffic or compute-demand growth alone.
Resource metrics are boundary equations: site water, source water, withdrawal, consumption and IT-energy denominators must be named before comparison.
The same facility design can create different water burdens across climates, seasons, water sources and electricity-generation mixes.
Cloud consolidation may improve allocation efficiency while reducing customer visibility into the physical resources behind purchased services.
Do not compare operator water totals without separating data-center use from corporate totals and accounting for methodology changes.
Technology comparisons require a common functional unit and life-cycle boundary; otherwise apparent efficiency can be a denominator artifact.
Reducing operational electricity can move the dominant burden toward server manufacturing, cooling fluids, construction materials or end-of-life treatment.
A modeled design advantage remains upstream of retrofit feasibility, supply chain, regulation, maintenance practice, operator adoption and fleet realization.
Per-functional-unit percentage reductions must retain the reference design, grid mix, lifetime, workload and normalization unit.
Jurisdiction-specific restrictions can displace data-center capacity and its environmental burden rather than reduce regional digital-infrastructure demand.
Technical feasibility and financing availability do not guarantee deployment when uptime risk, client preference, regulation, infrastructure and workforce are misaligned.
Facility efficiency can improve while sectoral energy, water, land and material demand grow with service scale.
Do not equate renewable certificates with physical grid decarbonization or ecosystem-wide environmental improvement.
Usable optimization headroom depends on operating load; placement flexibility and gains can attenuate toward saturation.
Optimizing heat recovery can migrate constraints toward latency, slowdown, network traffic, thermal cycling and scheduler compatibility.
Pilot measurement, numerical validation, simulated scheduling, advisory deployment, production control and net building outcomes are distinct evidence stages.
A larger recovered-heat fraction can improve local reuse without demonstrating lower aggregate electricity demand.
Do not report modeled improvement against random allocation as measured fleet-wide energy savings.
Workload growth, installed equipment and electricity demand can decouple because utilization, virtualization, equipment efficiency and facility mix change simultaneously.
A scenario comparison is interpretable only when it holds delivered workload constant while varying the efficiency and deployment regime.
Installed stock is neither active stock nor delivered service; facility-space type and operational state must remain explicit.
PUE measures facility overhead relative to IT energy and cannot by itself represent carbon, water, useful compute or lifecycle impact.
Improving a single operational metric can shift impacts across resources or lifecycle stages.
Metric choice is a model of the system: numerator, denominator, boundary, time and excluded stages determine the claim.
Climate-conditioned PUE comparisons require aligned weather, setpoints, control logic and system topology.
Agreement with another simulator validates implementation consistency but does not establish realized field performance.
Cooling technology can exchange electricity savings for water, cost, maintenance or heat-reuse consequences excluded from PUE.
Redundant equipment creates a designed reserve whose value is fault ride-through, not average utilization.
Commissioning must test integrated failure sequences and activation time; component presence alone does not verify system resilience.
Thermal ride-through is a state-dependent time budget set by initial temperature, airflow, thermal mass and fault scope.
The same cooling design can be highly beneficial, marginal or unsuitable across climate and air-quality regimes.
A modeled modular-facility maximum is not a measured campus-average saving.
Free-cooling performance must include the temperature, humidity, enthalpy and contamination control envelope.
Dispatchable facility flexibility is the feasible time-bounded change after workload and service constraints, not nameplate demand.
Peak-power reduction in kW and energy reduction in kWh are different objectives and can move independently.
Lab-grade control results require a deployment and contract-realization bridge before being treated as production capability.
Electrical, thermal and workload flexibility are separate products with different units, constraints and counterparties.
Waste heat becomes useful output only when temperature, timing, distance and a receiving heat demand align.
Operational pilots establish bounded technical feasibility, not campus-scale economic availability.
Data-center impacts are spatially clustered through land, grid, water, network and heat infrastructures even when services appear placeless.
A campus map or metropolitan inventory is a jurisdiction-specific asset view, not a national capacity census.
Policy approval, announced mitigation and heat-network plans are intermediate states rather than realized operating outcomes.
Facility environmental intensity depends on both site resources and upstream utility geography, which need not share the same watershed or jurisdiction.
Water volume and scarcity-weighted water impact answer different questions and must not be substituted.
Geospatial facility and server datasets are coverage-limited inputs; mapped presence does not prove complete fleet coverage or energized load.
Siting can improve one environmental dimension while worsening another, so optimization is multi-objective.
Whole-system circularity requires information and incentive alignment across design, manufacture, operation, reuse and end-of-life actors.
Awareness, participation, tools, prototypes and sector-wide material recovery are distinct realization states.
Extending equipment life or changing design can shift operational, embodied, supply-security and recovery impacts across lifecycle stages.
Small project-engaged stakeholder samples support process learning but not estimates of industry-wide adoption.
A facility inventory assembled from surveys, permits, websites and repositories inherits nonresponse, timing, definition and duplication risk.
A composite siting score encodes chosen criteria and weights and is not observed environmental performance.
Siting feasibility is co-produced by physical resources, municipal authority, ownership patterns and networked heat demand.
A municipal plan or incentive is an enabling state, not proof of construction, connection or operating integration.
A location inventory can support spatial-risk analysis while remaining unsuitable for MW or load aggregation.
Environment affects facility reliability while facility operation affects environmental burdens; both directions belong in siting analysis.
A flexibility claim must state direction, response time, duration, recovery, baseline and availability window.
Dual-purposing reserve assets requires preserving their primary resilience function and accounting for state of charge or fuel.
Tier or redundancy labels cannot substitute for coupled failure, degraded-mode and repair modeling.
New equipment adoption needs reliability evidence for the integrated power, cooling and IT system, not component efficiency alone.
Repeated citations of one original estimate are not independent observations.
Energy totals are comparable only after reconstructing facility types, geography, year, equipment and electricity boundary.
A sixfold estimate spread can arise from incompatible statistical architectures rather than uncertainty around one common estimand.
Standard energy reporting still requires facility and capacity state fields to distinguish planned, connected, energized and consumed power.
Manufacturing capacity, shipments, installed servers, current or in-construction building area, rated power and annual energy are separate pipeline states.
An open scenario with explicit assumptions is auditable but remains a scenario until deployment and operation are observed.
Waste-heat usefulness is a temperature-, distance-, timing- and sink-conditioned service rather than an automatic offset.
Heat-recovery technology suitability precedes retrofit feasibility, commercial integration and realized displaced energy.
Exposure pathway, modeled risk and observed health outcome must remain separate evidence states.
Local externality assessment requires receptor distance, timing and cumulative vulnerability, not facility presence alone.
A data-center water footprint must distinguish direct on-site consumption from indirect electricity-supply water and state the functional denominator.
Electricity portfolio, cooling system and climate can move most water burden away from the facility boundary, so local withdrawal is not a proxy for total water footprint.
A very wide modeled water-intensity range should be preserved as uncertainty and heterogeneity, not collapsed into an apparently measured typical value.
Economizer savings are conditional on climate, HVAC design, controls and the denominator used; PUE improvement does not identify the emissions outcome.
Facility siting jointly changes cooling demand and grid emissions, and these two location effects may reinforce or offset one another.
Modeled national technical potential becomes realized savings only through adoption, commissioning, compatible operation and persistence.
UPS batteries contain deliberately reserved reliability capacity; any grid-service estimate must subtract the reserve needed to protect the primary load.
Primary-frequency flexibility is bounded jointly by power rating, state of charge, response time, activation energy, market rules and protection obligations.
Modeled UPS participation requires compatible bidirectional hardware, controls, market qualification and a degradation policy before it becomes operating flexibility.
Mesoclimate can create material cooling-energy differences within the same broad market, so city or national climate labels can conceal site-level variation.
Savings in a recirculating chiller cannot be restated as total-facility electricity savings without the facility load decomposition.
A reference-facility site optimization remains conditional on the fixed IT load, equipment model, baseline site and relocation radius.
Climate-neutrality claims are comparable only when Scope 1, Scope 2 attribution method and Scope 3 value-chain coverage are explicit.
Operational efficiency and cleaner electricity can lower intensity while aggregate demand and embodied emissions keep total value-chain emissions above zero.
An illustrative single-facility scenario reveals driver sensitivity but is not a fleet forecast without a representative sampling and aggregation bridge.

candidate_universal_families.name: Physical and operational capacity-state decomposition
candidate_universal_families.working_definition: Data-center capacity must be tracked through distinct project and operating states rather than represented by a single MW number.
candidate_universal_families.required_state_chain: announced or proposed -> permitted -> under construction -> commissioned -> connected -> energized -> IT-ready -> occupied -> utilized -> delivered service

candidate_universal_families.name: Boundary- and denominator-conditioned facility efficiency
candidate_universal_families.working_definition: PUE, WUE, carbon intensity, utilization and functional-unit results answer different questions and are comparable only under aligned boundaries and denominators.

candidate_universal_families.name: Geographic and subsystem burden migration
candidate_universal_families.working_definition: Siting, cooling, grid, efficiency or regulation can reduce one local burden while shifting another burden across resource, subsystem, time or jurisdiction.

candidate_universal_families.name: Design-to-operation realization ladder
candidate_universal_families.working_definition: Modeled or demonstrated facility improvement becomes realized operating performance only through construction, commissioning, integration, adoption and stable operation.

candidate_universal_families.name: Unit efficiency versus aggregate infrastructure demand
candidate_universal_families.working_definition: Lower resource use per unit of compute or facility service does not determine total infrastructure demand when volume, density, quality and adoption change.

candidate_universal_families.name: Reliability reserve versus apparent utilization
candidate_universal_families.working_definition: Redundancy, thermal headroom and backup capacity are deliberately reserved states whose value is fault tolerance; average utilization alone misclassifies them.

candidate_universal_families.name: Contract- and time-bounded flexibility envelope
candidate_universal_families.working_definition: Dispatchable data-center flexibility is the feasible change over a defined interval after workload, SLA, topology, storage and thermal constraints, not installed or nameplate load.

candidate_universal_families.name: Measurement architecture and evidence coverage
candidate_universal_families.working_definition: Every fleet, capacity or impact claim inherits the coverage, boundaries, denominators, state definitions and selection mechanisms of its underlying registry or measurement system.

coverage_grid.construction_commissioning_and_ramp: MODERATE—commissioning, reliability and current/in-construction proxy limits covered; direct schedule data thin

coverage_grid.local_economic_and_environmental_externa: STRONG_INITIAL—environmental, planning and health pathways covered; causal fiscal/employment evidence remains scarce

screening_notes.candidate: Industry project-pipeline reports and live campus announcements
screening_notes.reason: Useful to deterministic runtime evidence, but not a substitute for qualifying whole-text academic rhetoric sources.
Directly relevant terminology but currently fail the journal and normalized academic-admission gates.

screening_notes.candidate: Environmental footprints of the data center service sector in Sweden
screening_notes.reason: Directly relevant and journal gate passes, but the accessible page exposed abstract and references rather than verified whole text during this pass.

screening_notes.candidate: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report
screening_notes.reason: Authoritative technical report, but the frozen academic admission gate requires a JIF-qualified journal source.

screening_notes.candidate: Data-center interconnection queue and phantom-load reports
screening_notes.reason: Directly relevant to current project state but available evidence is primarily regulatory, consulting or news material rather than qualifying academic whole text.

screening_notes.candidate: Subsidizing the Cloud: U.S. State Incentives to Data Centers
screening_notes.reason: Potentially valuable causal fiscal evidence, but currently a working paper and not yet admitted through the JIF-qualified journal gate.

screening_notes.candidate: Geospatial suitability analysis for data center placement: Texas

handoff.next_action: Run saturation challenge 2 on five additional new qualifying whole-text papers. Complete the domain only if novelty remains at or below two and no material gap reopens.
handoff.gap_assessment: The targeted batch closed the measurement, registry, municipal planning, reliability and externality-pathway gaps. Direct academic evidence for commercial construction schedules, interconnection queues, and realized local fiscal effects remains structurally scarce and must be labeled rather than filled with trade reports.
handoff.convergence_signal: The first independent five-paper challenge added fifteen useful atomics but zero new generalizable families; every result mapped into DC-U02 through DC-U08.
do_not_do: Do not call the domain complete before long-form and two saturation challenges.
Do not replace missing academic pipeline evidence with trade claims.
Do not aggregate site counts, building area, equipment shipments or published MW into energized load.

long_form_analysis.design: Twelve substantial passage analyses from two qualifying whole texts: one qualitative urban-governance case and one quantitative source-audit review.
long_form_analysis.source_selection_rationale: The pairing challenges substantive infrastructure rules and evidence-provenance rules simultaneously. It avoids mistaking repeated facility-efficiency papers for broad domain coverage.

sources.title: How data centers have come to matter: Governing the spatial and environmental footprint of the 'digital gateway to Europe'
sources.whole_text_basis: Open-access author/article text reviewed across framing, methods, empirical history, policy evolution and conclusion.

analyses.analytical_theme: Cloud abstraction versus local physical infrastructure
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: The authors turn the cloud metaphor inside out: outsourced computation still depends on locally sited power, backup, cooling and fiber systems, so digital services create geographically specific land and resource claims.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Reframes an apparently placeless service as urban infrastructure.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Links the service abstraction to named physical subsystems and their local utility connections.
analyses.inference_boundary: This establishes material dependence, not the magnitude of any particular site burden.
analyses.runtime_implication: Require a physical boundary and site/jurisdiction tag before interpreting a digital-capacity claim.

analyses.analytical_theme: Growth crossing infrastructure and planning thresholds
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: Rapid cluster growth became politically salient only after grid and land constraints collided with permissive zoning; the moratorium marks a change in governance state rather than a simple reduction in announced demand.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Explains how an infrastructure issue moved from passive support to active regulation.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Sequences growth, constraint recognition, municipal concern and permit suspension.
analyses.inference_boundary: A moratorium changes the permitted project pipeline; it does not by itself disclose connected, energized or occupied capacity.
analyses.runtime_implication: Encode regulatory events as state-transition constraints, never as equivalent to canceled or removed MW.

analyses.passage_location: Research approach and interview design (article pp. 759–760)
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: Because prior empirical urban studies were thin, the authors combined policy and industry documents, news discourse, observation and sixteen semi-structured stakeholder interviews selected through ecosystem mapping and snowballing.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Makes the case-study evidence architecture explicit.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Triangulates multiple source classes while reporting participant categories and recruitment logic.
analyses.inference_boundary: The design supports process tracing and perspective comparison, not statistical prevalence or causal effect size.
analyses.runtime_implication: Preserve study design and sampling mechanism so qualitative process evidence is not converted into fleet-wide frequency claims.

analyses.passage_location: Empirical analysis, renewable-electricity claims and local contestation (article p. 768)
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: Operator claims of high renewable procurement coexist with a power system where renewable supply is scarce and local residents contest who receives that supply; an accounting claim therefore does not settle the distributional question.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Contrasts industry environmental claims with territorial resource conflict.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Places procurement assertions beside grid context and community response.
analyses.inference_boundary: The passage does not prove that a particular contract caused additional renewable generation or displaced another user.
analyses.runtime_implication: Separate contractual attribution, physical grid mix, additionality and local opportunity cost.

analyses.passage_location: Conclusion, politicization and policy cascade (article pp. 775–776)
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: Resource and land demands remained politically muted until protests, journalism, utility complaints and expert reports made them visible; subsequent rules attempted to align growth with grid and land limits.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Synthesizes the mechanism by which hidden infrastructure entered formal planning.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Uses temporal process tracing from low visibility to controversy and policy response.
analyses.inference_boundary: The sequence supports a governance mechanism in this case, not a universal timing law for every market.
analyses.runtime_implication: Treat registry and disclosure coverage as causal inputs to governance capacity, while retaining case-specific calibration.

analyses.passage_location: Conclusion, rebound, temporal mismatch and cross-policy conflict (article p. 776)
analyses.analytical_theme: Local efficiency cannot resolve aggregate territorial competition
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: Facility greening and early circular initiatives do not remove the aggregate land and energy consequences of continued cluster expansion, especially where data-center investment cycles do not align with grid and heat-network planning.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Limits the reach of efficiency and circular-economy narratives.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Connects rebound, opacity and mismatched infrastructure timelines to conflicts with housing, mobility and heating goals.
analyses.inference_boundary: The passage diagnoses persistent governance constraints; it does not quantify net welfare or prove that all growth is socially negative.
analyses.runtime_implication: Evaluate unit improvements inside an aggregate-demand and multi-infrastructure timeline, not as standalone closure of the burden.

sources.title: Sources of data center energy estimates: A comprehensive review
sources.whole_text_basis: Author manuscript and journal text reviewed across framing, methods, modeling typology, results, provenance audit and stakeholder recommendations.

analyses.analytical_theme: Estimate reliability as a source-chain property
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: The review does not choose a single preferred energy number; it evaluates 258 estimates from 46 publications by tracing the 676 sources underneath them.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Moves the object of analysis from headline estimates to their evidentiary ancestry.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Constructs a source-level audit across a defined publication universe.
analyses.inference_boundary: Source quality affects confidence but does not mechanically determine whether a numeric estimate is high or low.
analyses.runtime_implication: Store source lineage and audit coverage with every aggregate estimate; a citation count is not a provenance graph.

analyses.passage_location: Modeling approaches: bottom-up, top-down and extrapolation (Joule 6, methods/review framework)
analyses.analytical_theme: Method class determines inputs and failure modes
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: Bottom-up studies assemble equipment and infrastructure components, top-down studies begin from measured aggregate consumption, and extrapolations project from a baseline using an assumed demand-energy relationship.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Provides a typology for comparing unlike estimates.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Classifies models by where measurement enters and which assumptions bridge to the reported total.
analyses.inference_boundary: No method is intrinsically accurate; each inherits distinct data gaps, aggregation limits and projection assumptions.
analyses.runtime_implication: Make estimation method a required field and route validation checks by method class.

analyses.passage_location: Projection analysis and horizon comparison (Joule 6, results)
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: Historical estimates can incorporate observed inputs, while future values require assumptions about shipments, efficiency and demand; the reviewed forecast range widens as the horizon extends.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Explains why divergent projections should not be collapsed into a point estimate.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Compares the dispersion of estimates by target year and distinguishes observed from assumed inputs.
analyses.inference_boundary: A wider range signals model uncertainty, not proof that every scenario is equally plausible.
analyses.runtime_implication: Attach horizon, scenario assumptions and uncertainty form to forecasts; prohibit silent mixing of historical estimates and projections.

analyses.passage_location: Source composition and peer-review audit (Joule 6, results)
analyses.analytical_theme: Authority cannot be inferred from a peer-reviewed wrapper
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: Only about 31% of audited sources were peer reviewed, while roughly 38% were non-peer-reviewed reports; a scholarly article can therefore rest materially on industry or grey-literature inputs.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Tests the evidentiary depth behind formal publication labels.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Counts and categorizes underlying sources rather than treating the citing paper as the only quality unit.
analyses.inference_boundary: Non-peer-reviewed data are not automatically false, but require explicit provenance and uncertainty treatment.
analyses.runtime_implication: Apply quality metadata at the atomic source/input level, not just the container-publication level.

analyses.passage_location: Source availability and private-data dependence (Joule 6, results)
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: The literature relies heavily on private IDC and Cisco inputs; some links are broken and some citations are too incomplete to locate, leaving calculations difficult to reproduce even when the headline paper remains accessible.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Shows how access failures propagate into estimate confidence.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Audits private-source dependence, link survival and citation sufficiency.
analyses.inference_boundary: Inaccessibility lowers verifiability; it does not by itself reveal the direction or magnitude of numeric bias.
analyses.runtime_implication: Track durable locators, retrieval date, access status and replacement/archive evidence as first-class fields.

analyses.passage_location: Recommendations for end users, researchers and policymakers (Joule 6, discussion)
analyses.faithful_paraphrase: Users should inspect publication age, estimation basis and visible calculations; researchers should expose data and model assumptions; policymakers should improve standardized measurement and disclosure.
analyses.rhetorical_function: Converts the audit findings into controls for three decision roles.
analyses.evidentiary_move: Maps observed provenance failures to practical transparency and reporting remedies.
analyses.inference_boundary: Transparency enables scrutiny but cannot substitute for representative measurement or valid causal design.
analyses.runtime_implication: Expose a compact estimate card containing vintage, boundary, method, assumptions, source availability and reproducibility status.

family_assessment.conclusion: The long-form readings add mechanism, method and inference boundaries but no ninth universal family. Formal promotion remains deferred until both saturation batches pass.

saturation_challenges.batch_design: Adversarial spread across water accounting, climate-sensitive design, UPS grid services, mesoclimatic siting and full-scope GHG accounting.
saturation_challenges.decision_basis: All fifteen observations instantiate or sharpen existing family boundaries. None requires a ninth family, and no previously closed material coverage gap was reopened.
saturation_challenges.rule_test: PASS: 0 <= 2 genuinely new generalizable observations and no material gap reopened.
